citation: Hong, T., & Fan, S. (2016). Probabilistic electric load forecasting: A tutorial review. International Journal of Forecasting, 32(3), 914-938.
verification_note: Crossref record matches authors/title/volume/issue/pages; abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: Tutorial review of probabilistic load forecasting (techniques, evaluation, misconceptions); it explicitly calls for reproducible case studies. The abstract does not discuss holiday treatment, so cite it as the load-forecasting review/reproducibility call, not for a holiday claim.

citation: Arora, S., & Taylor, J. W. (2013). Short-term forecasting of anomalous load using rule-based triple seasonal methods. IEEE Transactions on Power Systems, 28(3), 3235-3242.
verified_url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1409.2027 (open-access version listed by Semantic Scholar; not read)
verification_note: Crossref metadata matches (vol 28, issue 3, pp 3235-3242). Abstract summary read via Semantic Scholar (fetched through a summarising tool, not verbatim).
relevance: States that anomalous load on special days such as public holidays has received little attention, and adapts triple-seasonal methods with a rule-based treatment so that normal and anomalous (special-day) load are modelled in one framework; tested on nine years of half-hourly Great Britain load, horizons up to one day. A combination of two rule-based methods was the most accurate, which is a (weak) precedent for combining special-day treatments.

citation: Ziel, F., & Liu, B. (2016). Lasso estimation for GEFCom2014 probabilistic electric load forecasting. International Journal of Forecasting, 32(3), 1029-1037.
verification_note: Crossref and IDEAS agree on authors, title, volume 32(3), pages 1029-1037; abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: Lasso-estimated hourly load model whose abstract lists public holiday effects among the modelled seasonal/calendar components; reported to beat two multiple-linear-regression benchmarks taken from the top eight GEFCom2014 entries. Precedent for penalised (shrinkage) estimation of holiday effects in load models.

citation: Charlton, N., & Singleton, C. (2014). A refined parametric model for short term load forecasting. International Journal of Forecasting, 30(2), 364-368.
verification_note: Crossref and IDEAS agree; abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: GEFCom2012 parametric model; the abstract lists 'special treatments of public holidays' among refinements, each shown with competition scores to improve accuracy. Evidence from a competition setting that explicit holiday handling pays off.

citation: Banerjee, A., & Sarkar, S. (2010). Modeling regional electricity load in India (Working Paper Series No. 656). Indian Institute of Management Calcutta, May 2010.
verification_note: Institutional repository record (title, authors, WPS No. 656, issued 2010-05-01) and the working-paper PDF both read.
relevance: Hourly northern-grid load for 2005 modelled with AR(2)-plus-dummies (day of week, national non-Sunday holidays, season). The single pooled 'national non-Sunday holiday' dummy had no significant effect; the authors suggest private-sector factories and offices do not follow the gazetted holidays. Only Indian load paper found that uses a pooled holiday dummy; one region, one year.
qualifies_or_contradicts: QUALIFIES our claims. A pooled national-holiday dummy found nothing in India's northern grid. This can be read two ways (a pooled dummy washes out heterogeneous effects, or official holidays are simply not what moves load); the paper cannot distinguish them. Must be acknowledged, not hidden.

citation: Fernandes, R. S. S., Bichpuriya, Y. K., Rao, M. S. S., & Soman, S. A. (2011). Day ahead load forecasting models for holidays in Indian context. In 2011 International Conference on Power and Energy Systems (ICPES), pp. 1-5. IEEE.
verification_note: EXISTENCE VERIFIED (Crossref and Semantic Scholar agree on title, 4 authors, venue, year, pages 1-5). ABSTRACT AND FULL TEXT NOT READ (Semantic Scholar abstract null; IEEE Xplore page returned empty through the fetch tool).
relevance: The title states it models day-ahead load for holidays in the Indian context, making it the most on-topic Indian holiday-load paper found. I could not read what it actually does or finds, so obtain the paper before making any claim about its content.

citation: Bell, W. R., & Hillmer, S. C. (1983). Modeling time series with calendar variation. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 78(383), 526-534.
verification_note: EXISTENCE VERIFIED via Crossref (authors, title, JASA 78(383), pp 526-534). ABSTRACT NOT READ (Semantic Scholar null; other abstract sources blocked). The relevance note below is taken from how two papers I did read (Roberts & White 2015; Lin & Liu 2002) describe it.
relevance: As described by Roberts & White (2015): the Bell-Hillmer moving-holiday regressor is a dummy equal to the fraction of holiday-affected days falling in each month. Lin & Liu (2002) describe it as the method developed for Easter, which they adapt to lunar holidays. Foundational reference for moving-holiday regressors in official statistics.

citation: Liu, L.-M. (1980). Note - Analysis of time series with calendar effects. Management Science, 26(1), 106-112.
verification_note: EconPapers record read: authors, title, Management Science 26(1) pp 106-112, DOI and abstract all shown on the page.
relevance: Points out that holidays such as Easter, Passover and Chinese New Year follow lunar dates and so move between adjacent months, altering monthly figures; examines how this calendar intervention distorts sample autocorrelation and discusses model estimation. Early statement of the moving-holiday problem.

citation: Findley, D. F., Monsell, B. C., Bell, W. R., Otto, M. C., & Chen, B.-C. (1998). New capabilities and methods of the X-12-ARIMA seasonal-adjustment program. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 16(2), 127-152.
verification_note: Crossref and EconPapers agree; abstract read on EconPapers.
relevance: Presents X-12-ARIMA with more flexible seasonal, trading-day and holiday adjustment, including effects estimated from user-defined regressors, and regression with ARIMA errors plus model-selection diagnostics. Cite for the fact that official-statistics practice already allows user-defined, holiday-specific regressors (the 'typed' design).

citation: Lin, J.-L., & Liu, T.-S. (2003). Modeling lunar calendar effects in Taiwan. Econometrics 0306005, EconWPA, University Library of Munich. (Earlier version: Modeling lunar calendar holiday effects in Taiwan, U.S. Census Bureau working paper, July 2002.)
verification_note: Both the IDEAS/EconWPA record and the Census working-paper page were read; titles differ slightly (Census: 'Modeling Lunar Calendar Holiday Effects in Taiwan').
relevance: Models Lunar New Year, Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn festivals each with before/during/after regressors adapted from Bell-Hillmer, choosing the form by AICC and out-of-sample forecast accuracy on ten Taiwanese series. Finds holiday regressors improve seasonal decomposition, that effects are generally smaller than seasonal effects but should not be ignored. A per-festival (typed) design chosen by out-of-sample accuracy.
qualifies_or_contradicts: Mild qualification: holiday effects are reported as generally smaller than seasonal effects.

citation: Roberts, I., & White, G. (2015). Seasonal adjustment of Chinese economic statistics (Research Discussion Paper RDP 2015-13), Section 2: Seasonal adjustment with Chinese moving holiday effects. Reserve Bank of Australia.
verification_note: Section page read (authors, title, date shown as November 2015).
relevance: Chinese New Year is given its own Bell-Hillmer-type regressor split into three sub-periods (Lin-Liu), with sub-period lengths chosen per series by AICc (up to 20 days); Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn get their own dummies (up to 10 days). Chi-squared tests of joint significance are used per holiday and insignificant ones dropped. Clear example of per-holiday (typed) regressors with a pruning rule.
qualifies_or_contradicts: Qualifies a blanket 'typed always' stance: standard practice here tests each holiday's dummies and drops those that are insignificant.

citation: Taylor, S. J., & Letham, B. (2018). Forecasting at scale. The American Statistician, 72(1), 37-45.
verification_note: Crossref record verified. Abstract read via Semantic Scholar. I could NOT read the article's holiday section (PeerJ preprint page showed only the abstract); the holiday statements below come from the Prophet software documentation, which I read.
relevance: Prophet is a modular regression forecaster whose parameters analysts can adjust with domain knowledge (abstract). Per the Prophet documentation: each named holiday gets its own effect, can be widened with lower/upper windows, and holiday effects are shrunk by holidays_prior_scale (default 10, i.e. little shrinkage; lowering it dampens effects, and the docs example shows the Superbowl effect, the holiday with fewest observations, falling most). So a widely used tool is 'typed with shrinkage', a third option between typed and pooled.
qualifies_or_contradicts: Documentation, not the paper, is the source for the holiday details; cite the docs separately if you rely on them.

citation: Hyndman, R. J., & Athanasopoulos, G. Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.). OTexts, Melbourne. Section 7.4 'Some useful predictors'. https://otexts.com/fpp3/ (accessed 15 Nov 2026).
verification_note: Index page shows title, authors and '3rd edition'; the page does not state a publication year (copyright range begins 2012, last updated 04 Nov 2026). The conventional year is 2021 but I did not confirm it on the page.
relevance: Textbook treatment: a public-holiday predictor is coded as a 0/1 dummy; Easter, a moving holiday whose effect lasts several days, gets its own dummy (split proportionally across months for monthly data). Shows the one-dummy-per-event convention is textbook default.

citation: Das, A., Kong, W., Sen, R., & Zhou, Y. (2024). A decoder-only foundation model for time-series forecasting. In Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235, 10148-10167.
verification_note: PMLR page confirms authors, title, volume 235, pages 10148-10167; arXiv abstract page (v4, 17 Apr 2024) read. No DOI shown on the PMLR page, so none given.
relevance: Original TimesFM: patched-decoder attention model pretrained on a large time-series corpus, zero-shot accuracy on public datasets close to supervised per-dataset models, across history lengths, horizons and granularities. The abstract does not mention covariates (covariate support belongs to later versions, e.g. the TimesFM-3 blog you already cite).

citation: Ansari, A. F., Stella, L., Turkmen, A. C., Zhang, X., Mercado, P., Shen, H., Shchur, O., Rangapuram, S. S., Pineda Arango, S., Kapoor, S., Zschiegner, J., Maddix, D. C., Wang, H., Mahoney, M. W., Torkkola, K., Wilson, A. G., Bohlke-Schneider, M., & Wang, B. (2024). Chronos: Learning the language of time series. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2403.07815.
verification_note: ML Anthology and Semantic Scholar agree on title, 18 authors and TMLR 2024; TMLR has no volume/pages (none listed). I could not load the OpenReview page itself (browser check); the OpenReview id comes from the ML Anthology page.
relevance: Original Chronos: scales and quantises values into a fixed vocabulary, trains T5-family models (20M-710M parameters) with cross-entropy, on public plus synthetic Gaussian-process data; on a 42-dataset benchmark it beats others on in-corpus datasets and is comparable or sometimes better zero-shot. The abstract does not mention covariates; Chronos-2 (already cited) is the covariate version.

citation: Woo, G., Liu, C., Kumar, A., Xiong, C., Savarese, S., & Sahoo, D. (2024). Unified training of universal time series forecasting transformers. In Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235, 53140-53164.
verification_note: PMLR page confirms authors, volume 235, pages 53140-53164; arXiv abstract read.
relevance: Moirai: masked-encoder Transformer pretrained on LOTSA (over 27 billion observations, nine domains), handling multiple sampling frequencies and a varying number of variates; zero-shot performance competitive with or better than full-shot models. The abstract does not mention covariates or exogenous variables, only an arbitrary number of variates.

citation: Rasul, K., Ashok, A., Williams, A. R., Ghonia, H., Bhagwatkar, R., Khorasani, A., Bayazi, M. J. D., Adamopoulos, G., Riachi, R., Hassen, N., Bilos, M., Garg, S., Schneider, A., Chapados, N., Drouin, A., Zantedeschi, V., Nevmyvaka, Y., & Rish, I. (2023). Lag-Llama: Towards foundation models for probabilistic time series forecasting. arXiv:2310.08278 (v3, Feb 2024).
verification_note: arXiv abstract page read; no journal reference listed, so treated as a preprint.
relevance: Decoder-only transformer foundation model for univariate probabilistic forecasting that uses lagged values as covariates; strong zero-shot results and, after fine-tuning on small portions, state-of-the-art among general-purpose models. The page mentions no support for other exogenous variables, so it cannot take festival flags.

citation: Garza, A., Challu, C., & Mergenthaler-Canseco, M. (2023). TimeGPT-1. arXiv:2310.03589 (v3, May 2024).
verification_note: arXiv abstract page read; no journal reference listed. The page's citation metadata lists only one author but the visible author list has three.
relevance: Describes TimeGPT as a pretrained time-series foundation model for zero-shot forecasting, compared with statistical, ML and deep-learning methods on accuracy, speed and ease of use. The abstract does not say how, or whether, covariates are handled.

type: peer-reviewed conference paper (per arXiv comment) / preprint
citation: Ekambaram, V., Jati, A., Dayama, P., Mukherjee, S., Nguyen, N. H., Gifford, W. M., Reddy, C., & Kalagnanam, J. (2024). Tiny Time Mixers (TTMs): Fast pre-trained models for enhanced zero/few-shot forecasting of multivariate time series. arXiv:2401.03955 (v8); accepted at NeurIPS 2024.
verification_note: arXiv page read; the NeurIPS 2024 acceptance comes from the arXiv comments field, I did not check the NeurIPS proceedings. Volume/pages not obtained.
relevance: Compact (about 1M-parameter) TSMixer-based pretrained model; reports 4-40% better zero/few-shot accuracy than benchmarks. Notably it 'infuses exogenous signals during fine-tuning', i.e. exogenous inputs enter via fine-tuning, not zero-shot, which bears on how covariates reach a foundation model.

citation: Aksu, T., Woo, G., Liu, J., Liu, X., Liu, C., Savarese, S., Xiong, C., & Sahoo, D. (2024). GIFT-Eval: A benchmark for general time series forecasting model evaluation. arXiv:2410.10393 (v2, Nov 2024).
verification_note: arXiv abstract page read; no journal reference listed.
relevance: Benchmark of 23 datasets (over 144,000 series, 177 million points), seven domains, ten frequencies, short and long horizons, with a roughly 230-billion-point pretraining corpus built to avoid leakage into the evaluation sets; 17 models benchmarked across statistical, deep-learning and foundation categories. Standard TSFM benchmark and a leakage-aware design (pairs with Meyer et al.).

type: preprint (arXiv comment says NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track)
citation: Shchur, O., Ansari, A. F., Turkmen, C., Stella, L., Erickson, N., Guerron, P., Bohlke-Schneider, M., & Wang, Y. (2025). fev-bench: A realistic benchmark for time series forecasting. arXiv:2509.26468 (v5, 4 Nov 2026).
verification_note: arXiv abstract page read. The venue claim comes only from the arXiv comments field (which contains a typo); not checked on NeurIPS pages, so cite as arXiv.
relevance: Argues existing benchmarks have narrow coverage, omit covariate tasks, and use aggregation that may not show real gains. Introduces 100 tasks in seven domains, 46 with covariates, reports win rates and skill scores with 'principled aggregation with bootstrapped confidence intervals', and releases the fev library. Directly relevant to covariate-aware TSFM evaluation and to uncertainty in benchmark aggregation.

citation: Pineda Arango, S., Mercado, P., Kapoor, S., Ansari, A. F., Stella, L., Shen, H., Senetaire, H., Turkmen, C., Shchur, O., Maddix, D. C., Bohlke-Schneider, M., Wang, Y., & Rangapuram, S. S. (2025). ChronosX: Adapting pretrained time series models with exogenous variables. arXiv:2503.12107 (v1).
verification_note: arXiv abstract page read; only v1 and no journal reference listed, so cited as a preprint (any conference acceptance not verified).
relevance: Addresses adding covariates ('such as promotions or holidays') to pretrained forecasting models that were built without them, via modular components that inject past and future covariate information while leaving the pretrained model unchanged; also a 32-dataset synthetic benchmark for covariate-aware forecasters. Closest prior work on holiday-type covariates in pretrained models other than Kreusel et al.

citation: Micci-Barreca, D. (2001). A preprocessing scheme for high-cardinality categorical attributes in classification and prediction problems. ACM SIGKDD Explorations Newsletter, 3(1), 27-32.
verification_note: Crossref record matches (vol 3, issue 1, pp 27-32). Abstract read on a third-party aggregator (synapsesocial), since the ACM page could not be fetched.
relevance: Proposes an empirical-Bayes preprocessing step for categorical fields with many values; for hierarchical attributes it blends statistics across levels of aggregation. This is the origin of shrinkage-style target encoding, i.e. partial pooling between a level's own mean and its parent's.

citation: Pargent, F., Pfisterer, F., Thomas, J., & Bischl, B. (2022). Regularized target encoding outperforms traditional methods in supervised machine learning with high cardinality features. Computational Statistics, 37(5), 2671-2692.
verification_note: Crossref record verified (37(5), 2671-2692, published online 2022-03-04); abstract read via Semantic Scholar.
relevance: Benchmarks encoders for high-cardinality categorical features across lasso, random forest, gradient boosting, kNN and SVM on regression and classification data. Regularised target encoding performed best; integer encoding and 'leaf encoding' (reducing the number of levels, sometimes using target information, before one-hot/dummy encoding) did worse. Evidence that collapsing levels is dominated by a shrunk per-level encoding, at least for many-level features.
qualifies_or_contradicts: QUALIFIES the typed-vs-pooled framing: the winner is a regularised per-level (partial-pooling) encoding, a third option. Also concerns genuinely high-cardinality features, not 10-30 festival types.

citation: Probst, P., Wright, M. N., & Boulesteix, A.-L. (2019). Hyperparameters and tuning strategies for random forest. WIREs Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 9(3), e1301.
verification_note: Crossref record verified (vol 9, issue 3, 2019; article number e1301, no page range); abstract read via Semantic Scholar.
relevance: Reviews random-forest hyperparameters including the minimum number of samples a node must contain (node size) and how they affect prediction performance, and gives tuning strategies. Per the summary I read, the abstract does not say which direction node size should be set. About random forests, not boosting; use only as general support that minimum node size is a first-order tuning choice.

citation: Efron, B., & Morris, C. (1975). Data analysis using Stein's estimator and its generalizations. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 70(350), 311-319.
verification_note: Crossref record verified; article PDF (course-hosted copy) read for the claims below.
relevance: Shrinks each unit's estimate toward the grand mean instead of estimating each separately; in the batting example total squared error fell from 17.56 to 5.01 and efficiency gains across three examples were roughly 350%, 200% and 100%. The paper also notes shrinkage can increase risk for individual components (up to k/4 times the MLE risk), motivating limited-translation versions. Classic basis for 'pooled helps on average, can hurt individual types'.
qualifies_or_contradicts: QUALIFIES a simple pooling story: shrinkage helps in aggregate but can hurt individual components, which is the heterogeneity concern in our setting.

citation: Montero-Manso, P., & Hyndman, R. J. (2021). Principles and algorithms for forecasting groups of time series: Locality and globality. International Journal of Forecasting, 37(4), 1632-1653.
verification_note: Crossref and IDEAS agree; abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: Shows global (one model fitted across all series) and local methods can give identical forecasts without assuming the series are similar, and that global linear models were competitive with the simplest local methods while using far fewer parameters. Analogy only: it concerns sharing parameters across series, not pooling categorical indicators across festivals.

citation: Miller, D. M., & Williams, D. (2003). Shrinkage estimators of time series seasonal factors and their effect on forecasting accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting, 19(4), 669-684.
verification_note: EXISTENCE VERIFIED on IDEAS (authors, title, IJF 19(4), 669-684; Elsevier PII S0169-2070(02)00077-8, no DOI listed there). IDEAS shows NO ABSTRACT; the description below comes from the abstract of Boylan et al. (2015), which I read, not from this paper.
relevance: Per Boylan et al. (2015), this is a study of shrinkage estimators for seasonal factors in time series whose reproduction failed in two independent attempts, changing conclusions about when seasonal damping beats classical decomposition. Directly about shrinking seasonal indices (a pooling/bias-variance question) in an IJF paper; read the paper before citing its findings.
qualifies_or_contradicts: See Boylan2015: the original findings did not replicate.

citation: LightGBM developers. LightGBM documentation: Parameters; Parameters Tuning (min_data_in_leaf, alias min_child_samples; categorical parameters). https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ (accessed 15 Nov 2026).
verification_note: Both documentation pages read via the fetch tool (summarised, not verbatim). Document version/date not stated; cite the library version you used.
relevance: min_data_in_leaf (aliases include min_child_samples) is the 'minimal number of data in one leaf', default 20, helps against over-fitting, and because the check is Hessian-based a split can occasionally create a leaf with fewer observations. Tuning page: 'a very important parameter to prevent over-fitting in a leaf-wise tree'; blocks very specific nodes describing only a few observations; too large causes under-fitting; for large datasets hundreds or thousands is enough. For categoricals, cat_smooth (default 10) reduces noise for categories with few points and min_data_per_group defaults to 100.
qualifies_or_contradicts: CAUTION for the simulation mechanism: the threshold is in ROWS, not days. In a state-by-day panel a flag active on one day contributes one row per state per year, so whether it falls below min_data_in_leaf depends on panel size. State the mechanism in rows (and note the Hessian caveat).

citation: Diebold, F. X., & Mariano, R. S. (1995). Comparing predictive accuracy. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 13(3), 253-263.
verification_note: Crossref (JBES 13(3), 253-263, DOI above) and EconPapers agree; abstract read on EconPapers. Note a 2002 JBES reprint (20(1), 134-144) also exists: cite the 1995 article.
relevance: Tests of equal forecast accuracy that work for many accuracy measures including asymmetric or non-quadratic loss, and allow non-normal, nonzero-mean, serially and contemporaneously correlated forecast errors; asymptotic and exact finite-sample versions. Baseline against which the clustered sign-flip test is positioned.

citation: Hansen, P. R., Lunde, A., & Nason, J. M. (2011). The model confidence set. Econometrica, 79(2), 453-497.
verification_note: IDEAS page read (title, authors, Econometrica 79(2), 453-497, March 2011, abstract). The page lists no DOI and I did not confirm one, so none given; the abstract on IDEAS is noted as taken from another version of the item.
relevance: Constructs a set of models that contains the best model at a chosen confidence level, with size reflecting how informative the data are (weak data leave many models in the set); no model need be the true one. Alternative to pairwise tests for multi-model comparisons such as Ridge/SARIMAX/LightGBM/TSFM x typed/pooled.

citation: Cameron, A. C., Gelbach, J. B., & Miller, D. L. (2008). Bootstrap-based improvements for inference with clustered errors. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 90(3), 414-427.
verification_note: Crossref DOI record and IDEAS page agree; abstract read on IDEAS. (A 2007 NBER technical working paper, t0344, also exists; cite the journal version.)
relevance: Shows standard cluster-robust asymptotic tests over-reject when there are only about five to thirty clusters, and proposes cluster bootstrap-t procedures; in their Bertrand-Duflo-Mullainathan example a 10% rejection rate falls to the nominal 5%. Motivates using a small-cluster-valid test (family-year clusters) instead of asymptotic cluster-robust standard errors.

citation: Canay, I. A., Romano, J. P., & Shaikh, A. M. (2017). Randomization tests under an approximate symmetry assumption. Econometrica, 85(3), 1013-1030.
verification_note: Crossref and the Econometric Society page agree (Econometrica 85(3), May 2017, pp 1013-1030); abstract read on the Econometric Society page.
relevance: Extends randomization tests to large-sample settings where the data are only approximately symmetric, and applies them to a fixed number of clusters each with many observations; accommodates heterogeneous clusters and dependence within and across clusters. The theoretical basis for a sign-flip test over a small number of clusters.
qualifies_or_contradicts: Check that the family-year clusters satisfy the paper's conditions (fixed number of clusters, many observations each); the paper does not itself address forecast-loss differentials.

citation: Hemerik, J., Goeman, J. J., & Finos, L. (2020). Robust testing in generalized linear models by sign flipping score contributions. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 82(3), 841-864.
verification_note: Crossref record verified (82(3), 841-864, 2020); abstract read via Semantic Scholar.
relevance: A test that randomly flips signs of individual score contributions; often robust to misspecification (overdispersion, heteroscedasticity, omitted nuisance variables) and better at controlling type I error than quasi-likelihood methods; adjusted to be asymptotically exact when nuisance parameters are estimated. Supports sign-flipping as a robust inference device. It is about GLM score contributions, not forecast-loss differentials, so cite for the method only.
qualifies_or_contradicts: Method transfer caveat: not developed for forecast comparison.

citation: Franses, P. H. (2016). A note on the Mean Absolute Scaled Error. International Journal of Forecasting, 32(1), 20-22.
verification_note: Crossref and IDEAS agree (IJF 32(1), 20-22); abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: Supports Hyndman and Koehler's proposal of MASE as default metric by showing MASE can be used within the Diebold-Mariano framework; argues other criteria lack the necessary moment properties, with simulation experiments. Licenses using MASE loss differentials in a significance test.

citation: Koutsandreas, D., Spiliotis, E., Petropoulos, F., & Assimakopoulos, V. (2022). On the selection of forecasting accuracy measures. Journal of the Operational Research Society, 73(5), 937-954.
verification_note: Crossref record verified (73(5), 937-954; Crossref 'issued' year is 2021, i.e. online first, issue year 2022); abstract read via Semantic Scholar.
relevance: Reviews common error measures in three categories (percentage, relative, scaled) and, in a large empirical study using average ranked point-forecast accuracy, finds measures differ only slightly, especially within a category. Supports an argument that conclusions are not very sensitive to the choice among scaled measures; the abstract does not mention MASE by name or its limitations.
qualifies_or_contradicts: I found no verified paper specifically on limitations of MASE; this is the closest.

citation: Petropoulos, F., Apiletti, D., Assimakopoulos, V., Babai, M. Z., Barrow, D. K., et al. (2022). Forecasting: theory and practice. International Journal of Forecasting, 38(3), 705-871. (80 authors.)
verification_note: Crossref (80 authors, 38(3), 705-871) and IDEAS agree. I read only the abstract, not the sections; the page is 535k characters.
relevance: Non-systematic review of forecasting theory and practice: models, methods, principles and approaches for preparing, producing, organising and evaluating forecasts, and their application in real-world settings. Cite as the general reference for forecast evaluation practice; I cannot point to specific sections on calendar effects or evaluation from what I read.

citation: Hewamalage, H., Ackermann, K., & Bergmeir, C. (2023). Forecast evaluation for data scientists: common pitfalls and best practices. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 37(2), 788-832.
verification_note: Crossref verified (37(2), 788-832; print March 2023, online 2 Dec 2022); abstract read via Semantic Scholar.
relevance: Tutorial arguing that many ML researchers are unfamiliar with forecast evaluation, which leads to flawed practices that can make weak methods look competitive; recommends practices for data partitioning, error calculation, statistical testing and choice of error measures. Supports the paper's evaluation protocol and its emphasis on controls.

citation: Boylan, J. E., Goodwin, P., Mohammadipour, M., & Syntetos, A. A. (2015). Reproducibility in forecasting research. International Journal of Forecasting, 31(1), 79-90.
verification_note: IDEAS page read (authors, title, IJF 31(1), 79-90, DOI link, abstract). Not separately checked against Crossref.
relevance: Two groups tried to reproduce Miller and Williams (2003), a study of shrinkage estimators for seasonal factors; they roughly matched each other but could not replicate the original, and the gaps changed conclusions about when seasonal damping beats classical decomposition. Documenting methods with a flowchart is argued to reach wider audiences than code sharing alone. Direct IJF precedent for reproducibility of a shrinkage-vs-no-shrinkage result.
qualifies_or_contradicts: QUALIFIES: a published shrinkage-estimator result in this area failed replication, which argues for the pre-registered, code-released design.

citation: Makridakis, S., Spiliotis, E., & Assimakopoulos, V. (2020). The M4 Competition: 100,000 time series and 61 forecasting methods. International Journal of Forecasting, 36(1), 54-74.
verification_note: IDEAS page read (authors, title, IJF 36(1), 54-74, DOI link, abstract). Not separately checked against Crossref.
relevance: Reports the M4 competition: far more series, a wider range of methods, prediction intervals assessed alongside point forecasts, and computational demands per method; the dataset is expected to serve as a testing ground for new methods. Standard reference for open, comparable forecasting evaluations.

citation: Kapoor, S., & Narayanan, A. (2023). Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science. Patterns, 4(9), 100804.
verification_note: Crossref verified (Patterns 4(9), article 100804, September 2023); abstract read via Semantic Scholar.
relevance: Survey finds data leakage in 17 fields affecting 294 papers, proposes an eight-type leakage taxonomy and 'model info sheets'; in a civil-war-prediction reproduction, correcting errors showed complex ML did not meaningfully beat logistic regression. General support for leakage controls and for sceptical baselines; complements Meyer et al. on TSFM leakage.

citation: Morris, T. P., White, I. R., & Crowther, M. J. (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine, 38(11), 2074-2102.
verification_note: Crossref verified (38(11), 2074-2102; online 2019-01-16, print 2019-05-20); abstract read via Semantic Scholar (which lists 2017, an earlier preprint date).
relevance: Tutorial on designing, executing and reporting simulation studies, with the ADEMP framework (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, performance measures); a review of 100 Statistics in Medicine articles found room for improvement in practice. Gives a reporting template for the simulation that explains when typing helps.

citation: Smith, J., & Wallis, K. F. (2009). A simple explanation of the forecast combination puzzle. Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, 71(3), 331-355.
verification_note: Crossref and IDEAS agree; abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: Explains the combination puzzle (simple averages often beat estimated-weight combinations) by estimation error in the weights in finite samples, supported by a small Monte Carlo study and a re-examination of Stock and Watson (2003). A simulation used to explain an empirical forecasting regularity, and relevant to why a fixed 50/50 combination of typed and pooled may beat estimated weights.

citation: Wang, X., Hyndman, R. J., Li, F., & Kang, Y. (2023). Forecast combinations: An over 50-year review. International Journal of Forecasting, 39(4), 1518-1547.
verification_note: IDEAS page read (authors, title, IJF 39(4), 1518-1547, DOI link, abstract). Not separately checked against Crossref.
relevance: Review of forecast combination from simple averaging to time-varying and nonlinear weights, dependence modelling and cross-learning, for point and probabilistic forecasts, including issues affecting when combinations help. Updates Claeskens et al. and Bates and Granger for the combination section.

citation: Hong, T., Pinson, P., Fan, S., Zareipour, H., Troccoli, A., & Hyndman, R. J. (2016). Probabilistic energy forecasting: Global Energy Forecasting Competition 2014 and beyond. International Journal of Forecasting, 32(3), 896-913.
verification_note: Crossref and IDEAS agree; abstract read on IDEAS.
relevance: Reviews progress in probabilistic energy forecasting and GEFCom2014 (four tracks: load, price, wind, solar; 581 participants from 61 countries) and gives 12 predictions for the next decade. The abstract does not discuss holidays, so cite only as the GEFCom benchmark reference.

citation: Lan, Z., Liu, B., Feng, Y., Dong, D., & Zhang, P. (2023). Mid-long term daily electricity consumption forecasting based on piecewise linear regression and dilated causal CNN. arXiv:2310.15204 (v1).
verification_note: arXiv abstract page read; no journal reference listed.
relevance: Daily consumption forecasting motivated by lost accuracy on special dates; a piecewise linear regression with one-hot features for month, weekday and holidays, with the Spring Festival given special handling through a distance variable entered as a cubic polynomial, followed by a dilated causal CNN on residuals. Example of a lunar-calendar festival treated separately from other holidays; preprint, low weight.

citation: Makridakis, S., Spiliotis, E., & Assimakopoulos, V. (2022). M5 accuracy competition: Results, findings, and conclusions. International Journal of Forecasting, 38(4), 1346-1364.
verification_note: IDEAS page read (authors, title, IJF 38(4), 1346-1364, DOI link, abstract). Not separately checked against Crossref.
relevance: Reports the M5 accuracy competition on 42,840 hierarchical Walmart unit-sales series (30,490 point forecasts at the lowest level), with the setup, results, best methods and findings. The abstract does not mention holidays or calendar effects, so cite only as a competition/benchmark reference.
